newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Bears prevail in NZ debt markets at close.
newsitem.headline: Bears prevail in NZ debt markets at close.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against yesterday's close

* NZ bonds end softer, bearish tone feeds into money market
* Bill rates escalate on day but still below Tuesday's close
* Sentiment swings to hawkish on RBNZ economic forecasts
Bearish sentiment took a firm hold on New Zealand bond markets at Wednesday's close and fed through into the money market, undermining progress made at the open.

The 90-day bill rates climbed to a 7.68 percent finish, after rallying to 7.62 percent this morning as the currency's Trade-Weighted Index broke up through 69.0. The TWI softened to 68.94 from a intra-day high of 69.15, but was still well above Tuesday's 68.72 close.

"The thing has been struggling for days and days and days, and now the bond market woes have got the better of the short end. The short bonds have really taken another hammering today -- it has spread through into the futures market and made it pretty hard for the short end to rally," one dealer said.
"It seems that all of this week it rallies in the morning on the back of the TWI, which we've been walking into considerably stronger, and the afternoon just sells off again.
"I'd hate to see what happens if we come in to a weaker TWI."
The front futures contract ended four basis points higher at 92.29, and dealers said it was finding good offers in the high '30s and good bids down towards 92.25.
Dealers said there had been a lot of funding going on from one or two banks, and that after days of being in short supply, the 7/98 maturity had led the weakness in the bonds.

"They (the 7/98s) have been running reasonably special in the repo market. There's only one seller out there and he seems to have a bit of supply in them. So how long they'll stay special I don't know, if he keeps pumping them out into the market," one dealer said.

He said the market's focus was now on the Reserve Bank's economic projections due on March 13, and sentiment had turned hawkish after earlier optimism about the chances of a slight easing in monetary conditions.
Most players expect the RBNZ to revise its forecasts for underlying inflation upwards, saying housing market activity and import prices have not fallen away as the bank had expected.

"The widespread talk now is that the Reserve Bank will be reasonably hawkish on Thursday week, and it looks like the market is well and truly pricing that in. We're running very tight now -- today we're the tightest we've been over the quarter," a dealer said.
